label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Nana,

I wish I were sitting in the kitchen with you tonight instead of making Denise do all the talking. For one thing, if I were there, I could put the kettle on. For another, I wouldn’t have to worry about her doing a voice for me. Denise, please use my normal voice. Very distinguished. Very mature.

I’ve been trying to write this all week. I keep starting, getting a bit teary, and closing the laptop, which is not a particularly effective way to write a letter. Apparently I can deal with things breaking at work in the middle of the night, but writing to my nana requires several attempts and a recovery period.

There’s so much I want to say before you leave Kathleen Street, and I don’t want to make it sound like everything is ending. It isn’t. You’ve got a new place that you chose yourself, a big maple outside your window, and a crib league to investigate. There are people at Elmwood Terrace who have no idea what’s about to happen to their winning records.

But first I want to tell you what that house has meant to me.

When I think about summers there, I don’t see the whole house at once. I see the little television in the kitchen. I see dishes waiting to be dried and a baseball game I desperately wanted to stay up for. You had worked out an excellent arrangement: I thought I was getting away with staying up late to watch the Expos or the Jays, and you got the dishes dried. I still think I got the better deal.

I loved being in that kitchen with you. I loved that there was something ordinary to do while we were together. You didn’t have to plan an outing or keep me entertained. I could stand there with a dish towel and watch baseball and be perfectly happy.

I don’t think I understood then how much those evenings would matter to me. You don’t, when you’re a kid. You just assume there will always be another summer, another game on that television, another evening when you can talk your nana into letting you stay up.

I’m so glad I had all those evenings.

And I think about the back steps. You sitting there with your tea at six in the morning, and me coming out to join you. You wouldn’t talk until the cup was finished. I learned that rule. No point asking questions before the tea had done its work.

Those mornings are some of my favourite memories, even though I couldn’t tell you anything we did. We sat there. That was enough. These days, when there’s always something buzzing or ringing or needing an answer, I think you had the right idea. I’m considering telling work that nothing is officially broken until I’ve finished my tea. I suspect they’ll have concerns.

You raised half our family in that kitchen. Fifty-one years is a long time to make room for people, feed them, listen to them, and send them back out into the world. I was one of the lucky ones who got to keep coming back.

The house feels so much like you that it’s hard to picture it without you in it. I know I’ll miss it. I’ll miss knowing exactly where you are when I think about you up in Sudbury.

I’ll be thinking about Grandpa Walt tonight, too. He belongs in my memories of that house, right alongside you. I wish he could be there with you and Denise. I don’t quite know how to write about that without getting stuck again, so I’ll just say I love him, and I remember him, and I know there’s a lot to say goodbye to tomorrow.

You don’t have to pretend it’s easy for our sake. You can be excited about Elmwood and still have a cry about Kathleen Street. I’m managing to have a cry about it from Toronto, and I’m not even the one who has to move.

But I really am excited for you. The place looks nice. I like thinking of that big maple outside your second-floor window, and I want to see it for myself. I want to hear what you think once you’ve settled in, who you’ve met, and whether the crib league is any good. I hope it gives the Tuesday church ladies some competition.

Mostly, I’m proud of you. You looked at what you wanted, picked the place, and made the decision yourself. Nobody made it for you. I know choosing to move doesn’t mean you won’t miss the house. It just means you’ve decided there’s something you want next, too. I’m glad you’re letting yourself have it.

Now, about the crib board. I asked for it because I want something from the house that we can keep using together. Also because I’ve put twenty-seven years of training into this game and would hate to lose access to the equipment.

You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. Not once. Some grandmothers might have given a small child an encouraging victory. You apparently felt I needed an accurate understanding of how difficult life could be.

When I finally skunked you at fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I still remember how pleased I was. I’d beaten you properly, and we both knew it. The butter tarts were an extremely good way of acknowledging that. If you’re wondering why I’m still competitive with you, you did establish a reward system.

There are so many things like that I carry around with me.

When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me twenty dollars taped inside a card: “For pizza, you look thin on the computer.”

I love that you saw me starting a new job and living my grown-up life and decided the most useful thing you could do was make sure I had supper. You were probably right. You usually are about that sort of thing.

And last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner, you asked whether the internet was broken again and whether I’d fixed it. Now every time we talk, you ask, “Did anything break?”

That is honestly as good a summary of my job as anyone has managed. I could save us both a lot of time and put you in charge of explaining it to people.

I’m sorry that job is keeping me away this week. I’m primary on call, I couldn’t find anyone to swap, and I wish it had worked out differently. I wanted to be there to carry things and make tea and sit beside you for a while.

You don’t need to make me feel better about that. I know you understand. I just wanted you to know that being away isn’t where I want to be.

I’ll be up the weekend of December 5, once the rotation is done. You can show me your room and the view, and by then perhaps you’ll have an opinion about everything I should know. I’m looking forward to hearing it.

Tonight, though, I hope you and Denise take your time in the kitchen. Have your tea. Talk about whatever you feel like talking about. I’m glad she’s there with you.

Thank you for all my summers in that house. For the late baseball games, the quiet mornings, the pizza money, and the butter tarts. Thank you for teaching me crib, even if your teaching methods would not have qualified as gentle.

I love you, Nana. I can’t wait to see you.

December 5 weekend: you, me, the crib board, and our first game at Elmwood Terrace.

And don’t let anyone in that league wear you out before I get there. I want to beat you at full strength.

Love you.
